extracted.intended_audience: science journalists, journal press officers, institutional communicators, and science communicators interested in embargo practices
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and reported incidents about how scientific embargoes are handled, what counts as an embargo break, typical journal responses (lifting embargo, investigations, sanctions), and practical pitfalls (time zones, institutional press releases). Useful for press officers and reporters managing embargoed material.

rubrics_metrics.name: What constitutes an embargo break
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes what looks like an embargo break is not an embargo break at all — e.g., stories based on independent reporting rather than embargoed materials may be treated differently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the source of the information: if reporting used embargoed materials (press packages, advance copies), that is a breach; if it was independently reported and not based on embargoed materials, many consider it not an embargo break, though journals have sometimes treated such cases as violations (example: Pat Anstett/JAMA).

rubrics_metrics.name: Journals may lift embargoes after early publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals will sometimes lift the embargo early on a paper because of an embargo violation by a news outlet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an outlet publishes ahead of the scheduled embargo, expect the journal or its press package team to announce immediate lifting of the embargo for all registrants (example: Science lifted embargo after a violation; Journal of Experimental Biology lifted embargo after The Guardian published early).

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional press releases posted early can trigger embargo lifts
rubrics_metrics.description: A corresponding author’s institute posting a press release days before embargo is scheduled can cause the journal to lift the embargo early.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Press officers at institutions must ensure internal/external press releases are timed to match journal embargoes; posting official materials early is treated as a breach by some journals (example: Max Planck Institute press release led PNAS to lift the embargo).

rubrics_metrics.name: Wire stories published early may prompt investigation and possible lifting/sanctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Wire services running stories ahead of scheduled embargo times can prompt journals to investigate the circumstances and may result in lifting the embargo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wire services should be particularly careful with timing; journals may publicly investigate when a wire agency publishes early (examples: UK Press Association, Reuters stories prompting PNAS/other journals to investigate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions for embargo breaches can include revoked access or blacklisting
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals or meeting organizers may revoke press access or blacklist reporters/outlets after embargo violations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Potential consequences include being banned from future meetings (example: Reuters banned from an ACC meeting) or being blacklisted by a journal (example referenced: Pat Anstett and JAMA). Sanctions vary by severity and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journals may choose not to sanction if circumstances are explained
rubrics_metrics.description: A media outlet that breaks an embargo may avoid sanctions if it notifies the journal and explains the circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prompt communication with the journal after an inadvertent break can mitigate penalties; e.g., Reuters reportedly avoided NEJM sanctions after contacting NEJM about the break and explaining what happened.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press-package teams and aggregators investigate violations and communicate to registrants
rubrics_metrics.description: Press-package teams (e.g., Science Press Package Team, EurekAlert!) take embargo violations seriously, investigate circumstances, and notify registrants when they lift embargoes or take action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you are a registrant or press officer, expect formal notices and possible apologies when a violation occurs. Use official channels (EurekAlert! entries, SciPak notices) to confirm embargo status and any changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time zones and daylight saving changes affect embargo timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Daylight savings/time-zone differences mean standard embargo times may appear to shift for parts of the world, causing apparent early or late publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about time zone references when setting embargo times (including daylight savings changes). Expect confusion twice per year when clocks change in different places; plan communications accordingly (example: 'weird embargo time season').

rubrics_metrics.name: Attempted re-embargoing after publication is possible but may be reversed
rubrics_metrics.description: A journal may try to re-impose an embargo after something has been published (e.g., due to delays or confusion), but such re-embargo attempts can be reversed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If publication has already occurred, re-embargoing is often futile or controversial; journals may try then backtrack (example: PLOS ONE tried to re-embargo a paper after a delay, then reversed the decision).

rubrics_metrics.name: Media outlets have the right to decline honoring an embargo
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when asked to honor an embargo, an outlet may choose not to do so, and it is within their rights to publish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Press officers should recognize that embargoes are agreements, not enforceable legal restraints on independent outlets; plan for the possibility that some outlets will publish early and prepare contingency responses (e.g., lifting embargo, issuing statements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Meeting/award announcements carry specific embargo constraints requiring careful coordination
rubrics_metrics.description: Announcements tied to meetings or awards (e.g., Fields Medal, conference presentations) often have precise embargo times coordinated with organizers; misalignment across time zones can create problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate with meeting organizers and international reporters to ensure everyone understands the exact embargo/unveil time in multiple time zones; failures can lead to confusion or perceived breaches (example: Fields Medal announcement timing issues).
